newsitem.title: USA: Rubin downplays talk Fed culprit for stock drop.
newsitem.headline: Rubin downplays talk Fed culprit for stock drop.

text.p: U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin on Sunday played down suggestions that last week's interest rate increase by the Federal Reserve was responsible for the sudden swoon in the stock market.

"It (the stock market) did go way down," Rubin told NBC television's "Meet the Press" program. "What the causes of that, both the proximate causes and the ultimate causes are, I suspect is a much more complicated question."

The Dow Jones industrial average of blue chip shares plunged some 140 points on Thursday, or around two percent, on fears of rising interest rates and a sudden sell-off in the bond market. The stock market was closed on Friday.
The sudden stock market drop came after the Federal Reserve on Tuesday raised short-term interest rates for the first time in over two years.
Rubin shied away from criticizing the inflation-wary U.S. central bank, saying that the administration respected the independence of the Fed.
But he argued that U.S. economic outlook was good, with solid growth and low inflation.
"All the evidence to me suggests that inflation is likely to remain low," Rubin said. "But I also think one has to remain very watchful always with respect to inflation."

He also noted that intermediate to long-term interest rates -- which are determined by the market and not by the Fed -- are much more important for the economy than the short-term rates the central bank controls.
And those rates in turn will reflect economic conditions, which Rubin termed "very good."
"We have a very healthy economy," he said. "The outlook is good. We're really in a very good period," he added.
Rubin said he was open to suggestions by some lawmakers that the administration and Congress first work out a balanced budget agreement, then cut taxes.
"We're open to do that,' he said. "But," he quickly added, "I do think that we can afford and should have the moderate middle income tax cuts the president has proposed."
He also defended Clinton's decision not to support creation of a commission to correct the upward bias in the government's chief inflation gauge, the Consumer Price Index.
U.S. Senate Majority Leaders Trent Lott proposed the move as a way to help balance the federal government budget.
Rubin called the proposal by the Mississippi Republican "constructive" but argued that Clinton's endorsement of it at this time would have been counterproductive.

"If the president had come out and endorsed the commission at that point, that could have easily have created all sorts of politicization which in turn could well have forced this issue off the table," he said.

A Congressionally-appointed panel earlier this year concluded that the CPI overstates inflation by 1.1 percentage points, costing the government billions of dollars each year in cost-of-living increases on various programs.
